I certainly agree with the points about mouse use, but I don't think Apple is entirely wrong about this suggestion either. Indeed, there are more than a few companies now declaring the smartphone as the replacement for the PC. Desktop PC use has been in decline for some time because the need for their performance has become specialized to fewer applications and the chronic unreliability and encumbrance of their complex operating systems is no longer tolerable in a world where mainstream computing is now defined by a mobile device experience. That special performance is soon going to become the province of specialized net appliances.

We 'power users' tend to look at this from an ivory tower perspective. But the mainstream isn't using computers the way we do. The only applications that still require desktop system performance are triple-A games (which, I must point out, are only the proportionally shrinking head of a Long Tail game market now), 3D modeling, and video editing. Everything else is well within the means of mobile devices (and eventually cloud computing platforms) with vastly less cumbersome and breakable operating systems. I've been predicting the death of the traditional operating system for over a decade and I think it's finally getting there. Windows 10 is not just badly made, it's redundant. A package of junk 90% of users don't need or want. The increasing resistance to its adoption with each new iteration is not just a comment on Microsoft's poor engineering and marketing, it's a comment about the anachronism of the personal computing paradigm Windows represents. And it's not just Windows. Mac OS, Linux, you name it. They're all heading for this.

iOS most certainly has issues. It was originally designed around the notion of mobile hardware as a peripheral to Macs and to online services--for iTunes and the AppStore. It's not yet well suited to being a stand-alone device. But I doubt it will be that way for much longer and, right now, that's not so much of a problem for other similar products.

The future of mainstream personal computing looks like collections of PADs of different sizes (wrist watches to whole walls), various net appliances, and various cloud services sharing common personal domains. No one device is the computer anymore. They're all peripherals. The network is now both the computer and core operating system.
